messages.author: 952d759294773dd3
messages.subject: Line transects for sparrows
parts:
Distance lovers:
I'm working up protocol for surveying breeding Henslow Sparrows in
Tennessee. They are secretive grassland birds, but sing regularly and
can be surveyed adequately with line transects. I have several fields
where they breed, but I have a technical problem I have to deal with in
order to conduct surveys without violating assumptions of distance
sampling. The main problem is that some fields are narrow (~50m or
less), where we can only do one-sided transects where we walked the
transect line as the edge between mowed and unmowed habitat. I'm ok
with one-sided transects. I think I can deal with surveying narrow
habitats.
To build up to the question, I think I'm going to run a series of
one-sided transects at our 3 sites, which will deal with the narrow
habitat issue. The problem is that 2 large fields (300m x ~400m) have a
lot of firebreaks mowed lengthwise thru the field. Essentially there
are several 15-25m wide strips of "suitable" habitat (with standing dead
native warm season grasses) that stretch the length of the field and
then there's a 10m wide strip of growing blackberry and other greenery
not so suitable for Henslow's, repeat for 300m. I'm sure HESP's forage
in the greenery/firebreaks, but would not necessarily use it for
nesting. To add to the plot, HESP's are found in large fields of almost
exclusively green grasses that were burned the previous year (not
expected to be optimal habitat). So maybe the firebreaks aren't really
a series issue. My question is how to deal with the firebreaks and
unsuitable nesting habitat scattered between lines of suitable habitat?
Doing a point count isn't really the way to go for surveying these guys,
but a line transect would survey ample suitable and unsuitable habitat,
thus on a given transect, there would never be detections from 15-25m on
the length of the transect. Also, if we worked line transects, walking
the edge of the mowed/ummowed grasses would be best, but I'm not sure if
we violate assumptions of distance sampling because there may be no HESP
along the transect line. Thus we would technically get all the birds
along the line, but that is because there may not be any.

Thoughts would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks,
Scott Somershoe

State Ornithologist
Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency
P.O. Box 40747
Nashville, TN 37204

601-868-0101 (cell)

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Line transects for sparrows
parts:
I wonder if it is possible to put lines perpendicular to these features?
If necessary, cut a narrow strip, cutting across the habitat types. That
way, habitat type won't be correlated with distance from the line.

Steve Buckland

messages.author: 3908a2da5354fc44
messages.subject: Re: Line transects for sparrows
parts:
Scott,

I think Steve's suggestion to run your transects perpendicular to the
habitat strips is what you have to do. Even though only the warm-season
grasses are the nesting habitat, the birds are using the firebreaks as
well and I think you have to treat the whole area as habitat to be
surveyed. This is likely the preferred approach for the mowed/unmowed
areas as well.

I also have some other comments relevant to distance sampling and this
species. I have been using distance sampling to survey grassland
sparrows (Henslow's, grasshopper, and Savannah) for a number of years
and it works quite well. However, we only estimate the number of
visible, singing males because you need a song to distinguish among
species at longer sighting distances, and you need a visual sighting to
measure accurate distances. Their song is just too ventriloquistic to
estimate distance from auditory detection.

However, by limiting oneself to only visible, singing males your
estimate of density is biased low by the proportion of time birds are
not singing or visible. I have called this an 'availability' issue in
that only about 40% of Henslow's males are visible and singing during a
line transect survey - and distance sampling assumes all birds are
available for detection. I and my colleagues have a paper accepted for
publication in The Auk (January '07) that discusses this issue and
estimates the availability. The good news is that this availability for
Henslow's sparrows did not appear to change during mid-May through June
(unlike grasshopper sparrows) but I can't guarantee our estimates for
Pennsylvania would be the same in Tennesee. But at least you could
argue that this availability issue results in your density estimates
being biased low, and that this bias may be constant.

If you have any further questions feel free to contact me.

Regards,

Duane Diefenbach

Duane R. Diefenbach, Ph.D.
Assistant Unit Leader
Adjunct Associate Professor of Wildlife Ecology
